title: Sugar syrup stages, from thread to hard crack
subtitle: What the thermometer readings mean and what each stage sets to
excerpt: Heating a sugar syrup drives off water, concentrating the sugar until it sets to increasingly firm textures when cooled. Six stages correspond to specific temperature ranges. Thread is the lightest; hard crack is the hardest. Each stage suits different confectionery: soft-ball for fudge and fondant, hard-crack for boiled sweets and spun sugar.
sourceNotes: Sugar stage temperatures are standardised across confectionery and patisserie practice. Temperature ranges given are the commonly accepted approximations for standard sucrose solutions.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: hard-crack stage, 150 to 155°C, the highest stage in confectionery work

glossaryTerms.definition: 115 to 120°C. A spoonful of syrup dropped into cold water forms a pliable, squashable ball. This stage sets to the yielding texture of fudge and fondant.
120 to 130°C. The ball from cold water is firm but still pliable. Used for caramels and nougat.
135 to 145°C. The syrup solidifies in water to flexible threads that can be bent. Used for soft toffee, butterscotch, and candy brittle.
150 to 155°C. The syrup solidifies in water to brittle, snapping threads. Used for boiled sweets, pulled sugar, and spun sugar.

content.text: As a sugar syrup heats above 100°C, water evaporates and the sugar concentration rises. The resulting syrup sets to a harder texture the higher it goes. Each confectionery stage corresponds to a temperature range measured with a sugar thermometer. If hot syrup touches skin, run cold water over it for at least ten minutes and seek medical care if needed.
Thread, 105 to 113°C: The syrup falls from a spoon in fine threads. Used for sugar syrups and glacé fruits.

Caramel, 155 to 180°C: The sugar itself begins to turn from pale golden to deep amber as the sucrose decomposes. Used for caramel sauce, praline, and creme brûlée glaze. The colour tells you where you are: pale gold at 160°C, deep amber at 175°C, mahogany and bitter at 185°C.

Clip the thermometer to the side of the pan so the tip sits in the syrup without touching the base. Read the temperature directly. Do not stir once the syrup is boiling or you risk crystallisation. If crystals appear on the sides of the pan, brush them down with a pastry brush dipped in cold water.
